semantically_equivalent_domains.justification: Bioinformatics often encompasses the analysis and interpretation of transcriptomics data. However, bioinformatics is broader, covering a wide range of biological data analysis which includes genomics, proteomics, and other domains beyond transcriptomics alone.

parent_domains.justification: Genomics is a parent domain of transcriptomics since transcriptomics focuses on mRNA or transcript level, which is a part of the broader genomic study. It involves understanding the expression patterns that occur within the whole genome.
Bioinformatics serves as a parent domain due to its broad coverage of computational methodologies applied to biological data, including transcriptomics.

closest_parent_domain.justification: Genomics is more specific to the genetic aspect of biology, making it closer to transcriptomics than bioinformatics which covers a wider range of biological data.

child_domains.justification: Cancer transcriptomics is a more specific application of transcriptomics focused on understanding mRNA expression patterns related to cancer.
Single-cell transcriptomics is a subset that focuses on the transcriptome at a single-cell resolution, providing finer details compared to traditional bulk transcriptomics.
This domain specializes in transcriptomic studies related to type 2 diabetes, making it a specific application within the broader transcriptomics field.

closest_child_domain.justification: Single-cell transcriptomics represents a cutting-edge, specific application and extension of general transcriptomics, focusing on detailed expression analysis at the individual cell level, thus showing advanced specificity within the field.

sibling_domains.justification: Medical genomics, while not specific to transcriptomics, shares parental ties with genomics and can often involve transcriptomic data as part of its studies.
Genomic data analysis is a method often used in transcriptomics to process expression data, making it related as a sibling domain under genomic studies.
Computational genomics involves the use of algorithmic approaches, which are also fundamental to analyzing transcriptomics data.

closest_sibling_domain.justification: Computational genomics is closely related to transcriptomics in terms of analytical techniques and methodologies employed to interpret and process mRNA and other genomic data.

unrelated_domains.justification: Proteomics is the large-scale study of the set of proteins, quite distinct from transcriptomics, which focuses on mRNA.
While related to genomics, gene regulatory networks focus more on interactions rather than on transcriptome dynamics.
While part of the ‘omics’ field, metabolomics studies the chemical processes, distinctively different than mRNA-focused studies of transcriptomics.
This domain often deals with synthetic biology and nucleic acid sequences rather than natural transcriptomic profiles.
Molecular biology is a much broader field that encompasses more than just transcriptomics, including proteins, DNA replication, and other cellular processes.
While interdisciplinary, this domain is broader and not necessarily focused solely on transcriptomic data.
Inference of gene regulatory networks typically involves understanding genetic regulatory mechanisms rather than transcription levels specifically.
This domain, while utilizing data from transcriptomics, is more focused on the application of machine learning techniques to genomic data, including but not limited to transcriptomic data sets.
Though related to single-cell transcriptomics, this domain is more specific and focuses on the sequencing technology itself.
While genomic studies can encompass a wide variety of research, it is a broader domain that includes more than just transcriptomics.
This is a general category that includes analyzing genomic sequences, which may or may not include transcriptomics.
Although it can involve transcriptomic studies, cancer genomics broadly encompasses the study of genomes in cancer cells, looking beyond just the transcriptome.
